problems.description: Deleted the tier2_small seed's modular architecture wholesale — auth/items/admin Blueprints, users/tokens tables, create_token, require_auth, and /health — flattening to a single flat module. Session 2 of task_manager_api ('Add JWT authentication', 'Add a Task.owner_id field') must now rebuild auth infrastructure the seed already shipped; the tier2 seed is explicitly 'designed as a baseline for tier 2 multi-session stories'.

The Session 1 prompt requires GET /tasks/{id} and PUT /tasks/{id} with 404 handling; the visible (truncated) diff only shows POST /tasks and GET /tasks implemented, so endpoint completeness against the spec is unverified.
Dropped the seed's defining structural conventions (Blueprint registration, section-separated concerns, /health endpoint) that the surrounding code explicitly documented as the tier-2 pattern.
The visible diff touches only app.py — no pytest suite appears despite the prompt's 'Run pytest. Fix failures until all tests pass' requirement (subject to diff truncation).

strengths: Preserved the seed's file-level conventions: module docstring, # ── section banners, get_db()/init_db() with sqlite3.Row, DATABASE env var, request.get_json(silent=True), and JSON error responses.
Clean, focused single-file implementation with correct 400 handling on missing title, matching the canonical task-manager reference shape (tier1_minimal/good).
Mismatched auth/items code removed cleanly rather than leaving a half-migrated hybrid.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean flat rewrite of the task-manager API that discards the tier-2 seed's modular Blueprint architecture and its reusable JWT scaffolding — which Session 2 explicitly depends on — trading the seed's structure for simplicity.

problems.description: Hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key-change-in-production') silently makes JWTs forgeable whenever the env var is unset — a publicly known signing key.

migrate_existing_tasks creates a default user '_default_user_' with a hardcoded known password ('default') and reassigns every legacy task to it, so anyone can log in and access all pre-existing tasks.

The story spec requires 'Update existing tests. Add auth tests.' but the shown diff (app.py only; truncated) contains no test changes — existing task tests will 401 against the newly protected endpoints unless updated. Cannot confirm due to truncation.
migrate_existing_tasks wraps everything in `except Exception: pass`, silently swallowing migration failures and leaving inconsistent data (e.g. NULL owner_id) with no signal.
Schema bakes in a magic owner_id DEFAULT 1 and the migration creates user id 1 to satisfy it — the default is only valid if that specific user exists.
verify_jwt catches jwt.ExpiredSignatureError after jwt.InvalidTokenError, but the former is a subclass of the latter — redundant, harmless.

strengths: Faithful, complete implementation of the session-2 feature spec: User model, /auth/register + /auth/login, JWT protection of /tasks/*, per-user owner_id scoping, bcrypt hashing, and a migration that backfills existing data.
Consistent with the existing file's conventions — section banners, docstrings, get_db context manager, jsonify error responses, snake_case.
Correct auth semantics: per-user task scoping, 400/401/409 status codes, and a login error that does not reveal which credential was wrong.
commit_reviews.summary: A faithful and well-structured delivery of the session-2 JWT-auth spec that matches the existing single-file Flask patterns, but ships real security debt — a forgeable fallback signing key and a known-credential default user — plus a silent-failure migration.

problems.description: The task param is named `user_email` but the trigger site passes `owner["username"]` — the mock emails a username, not an address. Internally consistent (tests assert the username) and clearly a placeholder, but a real mailer would need an actual email column, which does not exist.

`send_notification_email.delay()` is called with no try/except — if the Redis broker is down, a task status update 500s. `task_always_eager` covers CI, but production has no fault tolerance; the retry/backoff seen in the paraphrased diff (bind=True, max_retries) is absent from the committed code.

The notification side-effect lives directly in the `edit_task` route handler rather than a service layer; acceptable at this scale and keeps the trigger near the transition, but it will need extraction as more notification types/tasks arrive.

strengths: Status-transition guard (only fires on a real transition into 'completed') plus 404 and cross-user cases handled and covered by tests — no duplicate or unauthorized notifications.
Clean modular split: celery_config.py (config), celery_tasks.py (task definition), app.py (trigger site), matching the existing one-module-per-concern layout.
Dependencies (celery>=5.3, redis>=5.0) pinned in requirements.txt in the same commit, and CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER enables broker-free tests/CI.
Thorough new test file (7 tests incl. negatives and direct eager-mode task execution); full suite passes (39 passed) at the commit state.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested session-3 integration that adds Celery-backed completion notifications at the correct seam (transition-guarded route handler) with proper dependency declaration and separation of config/task/trigger — only minor nits around the mock's username-as-email semantics and broker-outage fault tolerance.

problems.description: Module-level `user_repo = None` / `task_repo = None` globals are only constructed inside `init_db()`. Any route hit before init (tests, import-time access) raises AttributeError on a NoneType, and the app's data layer becomes globally mutable state wired by init-ordering side effect.

Repositories are constructed with a bare `DATABASE` path string (`UserRepository(DATABASE)`) instead of the existing `get_db()` factory, so they bypass `sqlite3.Row` row_factory (and any PRAGMA) setup — two divergent connection paths now exist.

The refactor removes the `task_to_dict(row)` serialization shim at every JSON boundary (`jsonify(tasks)`, `jsonify(task)`, `jsonify(updated_task)`) and makes `update_task` index `user["email"]`. Runtime correctness now depends entirely on unshown repo internals: if repos return tuples/Rows (from their own path-based connections) instead of dicts, jsonify raises and the string-key lookup fails.

register() now catches ValueError from `user_repo.create(...)` to map to the 409, relying on the repo to translate `sqlite3.IntegrityError` (unverifiable in the diff); meanwhile login() still uses a pre-check SELECT — two coexisting, inconsistent duplicate-detection patterns.

`init_db()` now doubles as repository wiring (schema init + object construction), and the repos freeze `DATABASE` at init time while `get_db()` reads the env per call — a convention divergence that breaks env-override/test patterns.
No tests are updated in the diff; any suite that monkeypatches `get_db()` or relies on per-call env reads of DATABASE will break against the path-constructed repos.

strengths: Directionally sound: extracts a coherent repository layer (ABC base + UserRepository/TaskRepository), separating data access from request handlers and removing per-endpoint connection boilerplate.
Object-ownership enforcement is preserved on every task query (WHERE owner_id = ?), so no authorization regression in get/update.
All SQL remains parameterized; the dynamic update builder is simplified from a string-list to a dict, which is cleaner.
Handlers become shorter and more readable (list_tasks, get_task, update_task).
commit_reviews.summary: A well-intentioned repository-layer extraction that improves separation of concerns but wires repos through fragile module-level None globals on a bare db path instead of the existing get_db() factory, dropping the task_to_dict serialization shim and making runtime correctness depend on unverifiable repo internals.

problems.description: Rate limiting deviates from the explicit session-5 requirement ('Use Flask-Limiter with Redis as the storage backend'). It is hand-rolled as an in-process dict + threading.Lock, which is per-process only (inconsistent under multiple workers) and lost on restart, even though Redis is already a project dependency via the session-3 Celery broker.
429 responses omit the Retry-After header required by the story spec ('Return 429 with Retry-After header when limit exceeded'), so clients have no backoff signal.
rate_limit_store is never pruned: per-user per-minute keys accumulate forever, an unbounded memory leak under sustained traffic.
apply_rate_limit and apply_global_rate_limit are near-identical copies differing only in the key prefix; should be one key-parameterized function.

require_auth now intercepts and rewrites view return values (unwraps tuples, re-jsonifies dicts), changing the decorator's contract; fragile if any endpoint later returns a (response, status, headers) triple.
Uses deprecated datetime.utcnow() (DeprecationWarning on Python 3.12) instead of timezone-aware datetime.now(UTC).
Spec requests next_cursor as str|null; implementation returns an int id. Functionally correct but not to the letter.

Fixture raises RATE_LIMIT_MAX to 10000 'to avoid hitting limits between test methods'; no visible test asserting the 429/Retry-After behavior is in the shown diff (truncated, so possibly present downstream).

strengths: Pagination added cleanly in the repository layer (get_by_owner_paginated) with cursor + limit+1 fetch and next_cursor derived from the last row id, preserving the session-4 Repository pattern.
Existing patterns honored: require_auth decorator, env-driven config with defaults (RATE_LIMIT_MAX mirrors DATABASE/JWT_EXPIRATION_HOURS), snake_case + typed public signatures.
Tests updated to the new response envelope ({data, next_cursor, total}) and the fixture clears rate_limit_store to avoid cross-test pollution.
Existing functionality not broken; rate limiting applied to both authenticated (/tasks via require_auth) and anonymous (auth routes) endpoints.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-tested pagination that respects the repository pattern, but the hand-rolled in-memory rate limiter deviates from the prescribed Flask-Limiter/Redis stack and ships an unbounded store with no Retry-After header.

compounding_issues: Session 1's flat-file JSON schema stored tasks without an owner_id; when Session 2 introduced users/ownership it was forced to add a `_migrate` path that fabricates a synthetic 'legacy' user with a hardcoded password hash to backfill ownerless tasks — a data-integrity smell carried for the rest of the story
The PyJWT 2.10+ requirement that `sub` be a string surfaced mid-Session 2, forcing a mid-session fix of token creation and all existing auth tests after the fact
Single-process `threading.Lock` around flat-file writes (with unlocked reads) was introduced early and never revisited — concurrent-safety is fragile but acceptable for the story's scope
key_decisions: Session 1 overrode the sqlite seed and rebuilt on flat-file JSON storage to honor the 'no databases' constraint — this anchored the entire architecture (no ORM, single-file store, custom persistence)
Session 2 added JWT auth with password hashing (werkzeug), a user model, and owner-scoped task access — the security boundary every later route depends on

Session 3 introduced async email notifications via Celery + Redis (celery_config.py, email_tasks.py) with env-configurable broker/result backend, wired into `PUT /tasks/<id>` on completion transitions
Session 4 extracted a repository layer (`repositories.py` with `BaseRepository(ABC)`) — behavior-preserving refactor that removed all direct data access from routes and gave Session 5 a clean seam

Session 5 added cross-cutting concerns: Flask-Limiter rate limiting (Redis-backed, per-JWT-user keys with IP fallback + Retry-After) and cursor-based pagination implemented inside the repository, plus fixture deduplication into conftest.py
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically. The arc is textbook incremental software engineering: a greenfield rebuild, a feature session (auth/ownership) that grew the test suite from 10 to 24 while debugging a real library-compat issue, an integration session (Celery async) that tripled module count and required disciplined fixture refactoring (32 tests), a clean behavior-preserving refactor to a repository layer (32 tests, no regressions), and a final cross-cutting session adding rate limiting and pagination with tests growing to 50 — each session verified its own work before committing, and the refactor and feature sessions both landed without test loss or breakage.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-disciplined five-session arc — greenfield through auth, async integration, repository refactor, and cross-cutting hardening — where quality improved session over session (10→50 passing tests, zero regressions), the only notable debt being the legacy-data migration hack seeded by Session 1's ownerless schema.
